extracted.intended_audience: patent applicants, patent owners, patent practitioners, and stakeholders responding to USPTO rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Proposed amendments to 37 CFR 1.321 governing terminal disclaimers to obviate nonstatutory double patenting, including definitions, required agreement language, filing options, and related procedural/administrative changes. Targets how and when terminal disclaimers may be filed and the enforceability consequences when patents are tied by terminal disclaimers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct tying via terminal disclaimer
rubrics_metrics.description: A terminal disclaimer filed in X(P) or X(A) identifying W(P) or W(A) as a reference patent or application directly ties X(P) to W(P).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example language and visual: W ← X. If a terminal disclaimer in X names W as the reference, X(P) is tied to W(P). Consequence: tying can affect enforceability when a claim of the reference patent is finally held unpatentable or invalid (see enforcement agreement requirement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect (transitive) tying via chains of terminal disclaimers
rubrics_metrics.description: Terminal disclaimers can create indirect ties through multiple intermediate patents/applications (e.g., W ← X ← Y ← Z), such that Z(P) is indirectly tied to W(P) even if intermediates are abandoned or pending.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If patents are tied directly or indirectly by one or more terminal disclaimers and the terminal disclaimers contain the proposed agreement, the enforcement of downstream patents may be affected if any claim in the tied chain is finally held unpatentable or invalid over prior art. The preamble gives chain examples and consequences (e.g., if a claim of W(P) is held unpatentable, then Y(P), X(P), and Z(P) may not be enforceable depending on tying and the agreement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unidirectionality of tying (no automatic mutual tie)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tying by a terminal disclaimer is directional: multiple patents can each disclaim to the same reference patent but not be tied to each other (e.g., X → Y ← Z means X tied to Y and Z tied to Y, but X is not tied to Z).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences are limited by directionality: if a claim in the central reference (Y) is invalidated and the disclaimers contain the proposed agreement, X(P) and Z(P) may not be enforced; but invalidation of a claim in X(P) or Z(P) does not affect the other patents unless tying exists in that direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required enforceability agreement in terminal disclaimers (proposed)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed § 1.321(c)(3) and (d)(3) would require that a terminal disclaimer filed to obviate nonstatutory double patenting include an agreement by the disclaimant that the patent in which the terminal disclaimer is filed, or any patent granted on the subject application, will be enforceable only if the patent is not tied and has never been tied directly or indirectly to a patent by one or more terminal disclaimers filed to obviate nonstatutory double patenting in which: (1) any claim has been finally held unpatentable or invalid under 35 U.S.C. 102 or 103 in a Federal court in a civil action or at the USPTO, and all appeal rights have been exhausted; or (2) a statutory disclaimer of a claim is filed after any challenge based on 35 U.S.C. 102 or 103 to that claim has been made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the core new enforcement limitation: a subject patent with the required agreement is enforceable only if it was never tied (directly or indirectly) to a patent that has had claims finally invalidated under anticipation/obviousness or where a statutory disclaimer was filed after a 102/103 challenge. The preamble provides multiple examples showing how this enforceability limitation applies in chains of tied patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Options to obviate nonstatutory double patenting without filing a terminal disclaimer with the proposed agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant facing a nonstatutory double patenting rejection may: (1) combine the conflicting claims into a single application; (2) cancel or amend any conflicting claims in the application or in the other application containing the conflicting claims; (3) argue that rejected claims are patentably distinct from the claims of the reference patent or application; or (4) file a reissue application of the patent whose claims formed the basis of the nonstatutory double patenting to add canceled conflicting claims from the application into the reissue application, provided the added claims do not introduce new matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are presented as practical alternatives for applicants/patent owners concerned about the proposed agreement. The preamble also notes an alternative of separating patentably distinct claims into another application and filing a terminal disclaimer (with the agreement) only in the application with indistinct claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative splitting approach for patentably distinct claims
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant may separate the patentably distinct claims into another application and file a terminal disclaimer with the proposed agreement in the application with the indistinct claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This allows applicants to avoid tying unrelated/patentably distinct claims to the enforcement-limiting agreement by moving distinct claims to a separate application that does not receive the terminal disclaimer containing the proposed agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Withdrawal of a terminal disclaimer before patent issuance (petition under 37 CFR 1.182)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the applicant amends the claims after filing the terminal disclaimer such that the claims no longer conflict with the claims in the reference patent or application, the applicant may file a petition under 37 CFR 1.182 to withdraw the terminal disclaimer prior to the issuance of the application to avoid the effect of the proposed agreement on patentably distinct claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After patent grant, a recorded terminal disclaimer will not be withdrawn (see MPEP 1490, subsection VIII). This is a procedural avenue to escape the enforcement limitation if conflict is resolved before grant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may file a terminal disclaimer — 'disclaimant' terminology
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed rule makes no change to who may file a terminal disclaimer but proposes to refer to the party with the ownership interest making the disclaimer as the 'disclaimant' rather than 'patentee, applicant, assignee, or grantee'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistent with 35 U.S.C. 253 and current MPEP usage; the proposed text replaces 'patentee’s ownership interest' or similar phrases with 'the disclaimant’s ownership interest' in multiple provisions of § 1.321.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit allowance to file terminal disclaimer in a patent (not only in applications/reexaminations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed § 1.321(c) and (d) would explicitly state that a terminal disclaimer may be filed in a patent (including patents not subject to a reexamination proceeding) to obviate nonstatutory double patenting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistent with MPEP guidance (MPEP 1490); when a terminal disclaimer is filed to obviate double patenting in a reexamination proceeding, it should be filed in the reexamination proceeding and not in the patent file.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminology and structural changes to § 1.321
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed changes include replacing 'judicially created double patenting' with 'nonstatutory double patenting'; referring to the patent in which a terminal disclaimer is filed as the 'subject patent' and the application as the 'subject application'; and identifying the patent or application forming the basis as the 'reference patent or application'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Other structural edits: redesignate existing paragraphs (e.g., add § 1.321(b)(1)(ii) to incorporate requirements in effect on September 15, 2012), add 'agreeing' to enforcement provision wording, and amend cross-references to conform with current MPEP language. These changes are primarily clarifying/terminology-alignment rather than substantive shifts in filing eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: No substantive change to when a terminal disclaimer may be filed
rubrics_metrics.description: The rulemaking 'does not propose to substantively change when an applicant or patent owner may file a terminal disclaimer under § 1.321.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The principal change proposed is to the enforcement provision language requiring the additional agreement; timing/eligibility to file remains as prior practice (though wording and definitions are clarified).

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement-triggering events (final invalidation or post-challenge statutory disclaimer)
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed agreement conditions enforceability on whether any patent tied (directly or indirectly) had: (1) any claim finally held unpatentable or invalid under 35 U.S.C. 102 or 103 by a Federal court in a civil action or by the USPTO, with all appeal rights exhausted; or (2) a statutory disclaimer of a claim filed after any challenge based on 35 U.S.C. 102 or 103 to that claim has been made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule focuses on final, exhausted adjudications or post-challenge statutory disclaimers as the events that can render tied patents unenforceable under the required agreement. Examples in the preamble illustrate propagation of unenforceability through tied patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO small-entity size standard for RFA analyses (USPTO-specific)
rubrics_metrics.description: For RFA purposes, USPTO defines a small business concern as: (a) whose number of employees, including affiliates, does not exceed 500 persons; and (b) which has not assigned, granted, conveyed, or licensed (and is under no obligation to do so) any rights in the invention to any person who made it and could not be classified as an independent inventor, or to any concern that would not qualify as a nonprofit organization or a small business concern under this definition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This USPTO alternate small-entity standard is used for cost/impact estimates under the Regulatory Flexibility Act certification and for estimating how many applicants might forgo filing terminal disclaimers containing the proposed agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information-collection and procedural impacts (forms and PRA/O MB control)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed new information collection (OMB control number 0651–NEW) for terminal disclaimers; affected forms include PTO/AIA/25, PTO/SB/25, PTO/SB/25a, PTO/AIA/26, PTO/SB/26, PTO/SB/26a, PTO/AIA/63, and PTO/SB/63. Frequency: on occasion; respondent obligation: required to obtain or retain benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preamble provides estimated respondent counts, burden hours, and fee impacts (estimates adjusted to account for an anticipated 20% reduction in filings of terminal disclaimers containing the proposed agreement). The USPTO solicits PRA comments on collection necessity, burden, clarity, and opportunities to reduce burden (e.g., electronic submission).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule classification and notice-and-comment posture
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO describes the changes as involving rules of agency practice and procedure and/or interpretive rules and states such changes do not require notice-and-comment rulemaking, but the Office is publishing the proposed rule for public comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citations to precedent (Perez v. Mortg. Bankers Ass'n, Cooper Techs., JEM Broadcasting) support the interpretive/practice characterization; nevertheless, the USPTO seeks public input on the proposed amendments.
